claim: Anthropic has been valued at close to $1 trillion [in a funding round around May 2026]
quote: valued at close to $1 trillion
evidence: Anthropic raised $65B on 2026-05-28 at a $965B valuation (up from $350B three months earlier), reported independently by Bloomberg (named lead investors: Altimeter, Dragoneer, Greenoaks, Sequoia) and CNBC [2 URLs -> 2 origins, both citing the same disclosed round but independently sourced]. $965B rounds to 'close to $1 trillion.'

claim: Anthropic's annualized revenue in January [2025] was 'in the low single billions'
quote: its annualized revenue was in the low single billions
evidence: Widely reported run-rate trajectory has Anthropic at ~$1B annualized revenue in January 2025, matching 'low single billions.' Capped at plausible rather than confirmed because the figure is Anthropic's own self-reported run-rate, not an audited number -- a source about itself is tier 4 regardless of which outlet relays it.

claim: Anthropic reported $47 billion of annualized revenue by [May 2026]
quote: By this May, it reported $47 billion.
evidence: Multiple outlets report the same $47B run-rate disclosed in early May 2026 [2 URLs -> 1 origin: Anthropic's own investor disclosure]. Number matches, but it is Anthropic self-reporting its own metric pre-IPO, not an audited figure -- tier-4 ceiling caps this at plausible, not confirmed.

claim: Third-party trackers currently put Anthropic's annualized revenue at around $74 billion [as of late July 2026]
quote: currently put Anthropic at around $74 billion of annualized revenue
evidence: A third-party tracker (TickerTrends, via KuCoin) put Anthropic's ARR at $74.1B in July 2026, matching the claim closely. This diverges from Anthropic's own investor-disclosed figure of $65B for the same period (CNBC/Bloomberg, 2026-08-17) -- the video correctly flags this as an estimate, not an audited number, which is itself the right caveat.

claim: Anthropic's revenue growth rate was 'roughly 51% per month' in May [2026] and had slowed to 'roughly 8% a month' by July [2026]
quote: growing at roughly 51% per month per month
evidence: Shown sum from reported run-rates: April $30B to May $47B = +56.7%/month (close to the claimed 51%); tracker June $69.6B to July $74.1B = +6.5%/month (close to the claimed 8%). Direction and rough magnitude of the deceleration both check out, though the exact 51%/8% figures aren't independently pinned to one named report.

claim: A revenue tracker showed Anthropic's annualized revenue at $54 billion in late May [2026], $67 billion in early June, $70 billion in mid-June, then a dip, then $71 billion, then $74 billion
quote: 54 billion in late May, 67 in early June, 70 in mid-June, then a wobble backwards, then 71, then 74
evidence: Endpoints match public tracker data (May ~$47-54B, June ~$69.6B, July $74.1B); the specific intermediate weekly reads (67, 70, 71) and the 'wobble backwards' aren't independently confirmable from the sources found, but the overall trend and endpoints line up.

claim: Somewhere between $3 trillion and $4 trillion has reportedly been poured into the American AI industry [as of mid-2026], across data centers, chips and power deals
quote: somewhere between three and four trillion dollars has reportedly been poured into the American AI industry
evidence: Press coverage in 2026 does use $3-3.6T figures for the AI data-center buildout, but the figure is more often framed as the financing need through 2030 (Reuters/JPMorgan) than money already disbursed. Actual big-tech capex to date is smaller (~$1-2T cumulative); the claim's 'reportedly' hedge and 'poured into' phrasing blend committed/planned spend with cash already spent, which real coverage does too -- plausible as commonly reported, not as a precise present-tense actual.

claim: The majority of the $3-4 trillion poured into American AI infrastructure is reportedly debt -- corporate bonds, borrowed money
quote: the majority of it is reportedly debt, corporate bonds, borrowed money
evidence: Goldman Sachs and CreditSights both put debt-funded capex at roughly a third (32-35%) in 2026, rising toward 35% in 2027 -- a large and fast-growing share, but not a majority. 'The majority of it is debt' overstates a real trend (single-digit-percent debt share just a couple of years ago, now ~33%) into a claim the cited analysts don't support.

claim: On $2-3 trillion of AI-industry debt at a 'perfectly normal corporate bond rate of three to four percent,' the interest alone works out to roughly $100 billion a year
quote: the interest alone works out to roughly 100 billion dollars a year
evidence: Shown sum: $2-3T x 3-4% = $60-120B/yr, so 'roughly $100B' is a fair midpoint of that range -- the arithmetic is correct for the stated rate. But 2026 bond-market reporting has investment-grade AI infrastructure debt pricing at 4-4.5% coupons and high-yield tranches at 7-9%, both above the video's 3-4% assumption; a more realistic blended rate would put the interest bill meaningfully above $100B. Sound arithmetic on an optimistic input is misleading, not confirmed.

claim: There is roughly a $10 trillion-dollar white-collar wage economy in America
quote: the roughly 10 trillion-dollar white-collar wage economy
evidence: BLS puts total US covered wages at $12.3 trillion (2025, all occupations). No primary source isolates a 'white-collar' subtotal at exactly $10T, but that would require white-collar pay to be ~81% of all US wages, which is plausible-to-high depending on definition rather than confirmed by a named figure.

claim: To make the economics work, AI would need to profitably replace the equivalent of about 10 million American white-collar workers every year
quote: the equivalent of replacing something like 10 million American white-collar workers every single year
evidence: Shown sum: the content's own logic needs ~$1T/yr revenue (claim 9's chain) out of a ~$10T pool (claim 10) = 10% capture; translating that 10% into '10 million workers' implicitly assumes ~$100K of revenue per replaced worker, a reasonable but unstated proxy. The arithmetic is internally consistent, but it inherits the uncertainty of the claims it rests on rather than standing as independently confirmed.

claim: Chinese AI labs, with a fraction of America's computing power, have produced open models that are by most measures slightly behind, level with, or occasionally ahead of the best American systems
quote: Chinese labs with a fraction of America's computing power have produced open models that are by most measures slightly behind, level with, or occasionally ahead of the best American systems
evidence: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 (July 2026) trails only Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on major benchmark indices while beating other US flagship-tier models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5) on coding and agent tasks -- matches 'slightly behind, level with, or occasionally ahead' closely.

claim: Chinese open models now reportedly account for more than 60% of all tokens used by American firms [on OpenRouter, mid-2026]
quote: Chinese open models now reportedly account for more than 60% of all tokens used by American firms
evidence: Multiple July 2026 reports put Chinese models' share of US OpenRouter token traffic in the 58-63% range (CNBC ~60%, GuruFocus 63%, ZUKCLOUD 61%), corroborating 'more than 60%.' An earlier/different-methodology estimate put it at 46%, showing the number moves with measurement window.

claim: A compressed Chinese model called Qwen reportedly performs on par with American flagship models from about a year earlier, while running on a machine that fits under a desk
quote: a compressed Chinese model called Qwen, reportedly performs on par with the American flagship models of barely a year ago on a machine that fits under a desk
evidence: 2026 local-LLM guides report dense Qwen models (e.g. Qwen 3.5/3.6 27B) running on a single consumer GPU or a MacBook while matching GPT-4o/GPT-4-class benchmarks -- consistent with the claim. Best reachable sources are enthusiast/trade guides rather than a corrections-desk outlet, so this is capped at plausible under the tier-4 ceiling rather than confirmed.

claim: A recent survey of thousands of companies reportedly found that over 70% of the AI customer-service agents that went live had to be rolled back or shut down over mistakes and miscommunications
quote: A recent survey of thousands of companies reportedly found that over 70% of the AI customer service agents that went live had to be rolled back or shut down over mistakes and miscommunications
evidence: A May 2026 survey of 2,527 enterprise decision-makers, commissioned by communications firm Sinch, found 74% had rolled back or shut down AI customer-communications agents -- matches 'over 70%' [many outlets carried this, including syndicated wire copy on several local-news sites -> 1 origin: the Sinch-commissioned survey]. Sinch has a commercial interest in traditional messaging looking better than AI agents, worth noting, but the survey itself and its methodology (2,527 respondents, 10 countries) are independently reported.

claim: Across the whole economy, the most optimistic estimates put genuine AI job replacement at something under 100,000 workers a year
quote: the most optimistic estimates put genuine AI job replacement at something under 100,000 workers a year
evidence: Credible institutional estimates for 2026 run well above 100,000/year: Goldman Sachs ~192,000/year net (16,000/month), and tracked AI-cited layoffs/projections in the 150,000-500,000/year range. The claim's implied ceiling understates the more commonly cited estimates, even though the broader point -- that actual displacement is nowhere near 10 million/year -- still holds under any of these numbers.

claim: The AI industry's job-replacement business plan (10 million workers/year) is running at something under 100,000/year -- 'not a rounding error,' 'off by a factor of 100'
quote: That is not a rounding error. That is off by a factor of 100.
evidence: Shown sum: 10,000,000 / 100,000 = 100, so the arithmetic is correct given the stated inputs. But claim 16's <100,000 figure is itself an understatement of the more commonly cited 150,000-500,000/year estimates, which would put the real factor closer to 20-65x rather than 100x. Still a large miss either way, but the specific '100x' is an artifact of the low-balled input.

claim: Most of the big AI labs reportedly lose money on every single request served
quote: most of the big labs reportedly lose money on every single request served
evidence: True of OpenAI (spent 50% of revenue on inference plus 75% on training compute; lost $5B on $9B revenue). But by 2026 Anthropic -- the video's own subject -- is reported to have reached ~60% gross margin, up from -94% in 2024, i.e. no longer losing money on the marginal request served. 'Most of the big labs' averages over a picture that no longer holds for the company the whole video is about.

claim: The bosses of the big AI labs [e.g. Sam Altman and Dario Amodei] spent years touring podcasts and conferences prophesying that huge swaths of white-collar jobs will simply vanish
quote: spent years touring podcasts and conferences solemnly prophesying that huge swaths of jobs will simply vanish
evidence: Well documented: Dario Amodei repeatedly warned (2025-2026) that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs within 1-5 years and unemployment could spike 10-20%; Sam Altman has made comparable public statements. Matches the claim closely.

claim: AI industry leaders are reportedly asking Washington for financial support -- loan guarantees and backstops
quote: the same leaders are reportedly asking Washington for financial support, loan guarantees, backstops
evidence: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar (Nov 2025) said the industry needed a government 'backstop' to improve financing terms for chip/data-center debt; OpenAI had earlier written to the White House OSTP requesting tax credits and loan vehicles. Sam Altman later publicly disclaimed wanting guarantees, so the ask is real but contested even within the industry -- the claim is accurate as 'reportedly asking,' not as a settled industry position.

claim: There is a rush toward stock-market listings at some of the most aggressive valuations ever attempted, aimed squarely at ordinary retail investors
quote: a rush towards stock market listings at some of the most aggressive valuations ever attempted. Dream-priced offerings aimed squarely at the ordinary retail
evidence: 2026 saw OpenAI targeting a ~$1T IPO valuation, Anthropic filing a confidential S-1 at a ~$965B valuation, and SpaceX's June 2026 IPO carving out roughly triple the standard retail allocation (~30% vs the usual 5-10%) -- matches the described pattern of aggressive valuations pitched hard at retail.

claim: Anthropic's [~$1 trillion] valuation is a price tag near the entire yearly economic output of Switzerland
quote: A price tag near the entire yearly economic output of Switzerland
evidence: Switzerland's nominal GDP was approximately $1.04-1.06 trillion in 2025, closely matching Anthropic's ~$965B-and-rising valuation -- the comparison is apt.

claim: AI industry leaders who spent years promising a 'job apocalypse' have reportedly begun walking that language back toward softer terms like augmenting and empowering workers
quote: have reportedly begun gently, carefully walking it back
evidence: Fortune (May 2026): 'Dario Amodei spent last year warning of an AI white-collar bloodbath. Now he's changing the narrative' -- directly corroborates the described rhetorical shift from apocalyptic warnings to softer framing.
